sections.name: Rigid Body Physics
sections.explanation_simple: Rigid body physics makes objects fall, bounce, and collide like in the real world. Think of it as giving objects the properties of solid physical things - they have mass (a feather vs a bowling ball), velocity (how fast they're moving), and forces (gravity pushing down, wind pushing sideways). The game engine calculates all this 60 times per second.
key_concepts: Newton's Laws: Force = mass * acceleration
Gravity: 9.81 m/s^2 downward constant force
Velocity: Speed with direction (vector)
Integration: Calculating position change over time (Euler, Verlet, RK4)
Collision: Two objects cannot occupy the same space
Impulse: Instant velocity change when objects collide
Friction: Force opposing sliding motion
Restitution: Bounciness (0 = no bounce, 1 = perfect bounce)

sections.name: Behavior Trees for Game AI
sections.explanation_simple: Behavior Trees are the most popular way to program game AI. Think of them as flowcharts for decision making. An enemy soldier might have a tree like: 'Can I see the player?' -> Yes: 'Shoot at player', No: 'Patrol waypoints'. The tree runs every frame and checks conditions. Big games like Halo, Alien Isolation, and The Last of Us use behavior trees for their AI. They're better than state machines because they're easier to expand and debug.
key_concepts: Root: Entry point of the tree
Sequence: Runs children in order until one fails (AND gate)
Selector: Runs children until one succeeds (OR gate)
Condition: Checks if something is true (can see player, ammo > 0)
Action: Does something (move to position, play animation, shoot)
Decorator: Modifies a child's behavior (loop, timeout, invert)
Blackboard: Shared memory where AI reads/writes data (target position, alert state)
Parallel: Runs multiple children at the same time

sections.name: A* Pathfinding
sections.explanation_simple: A* (A-star) is the algorithm that makes game characters find their way around obstacles. It's like GPS navigation for your AI - it finds the shortest path from point A to point B while avoiding walls. It works by exploring paths in order of promise: it checks the most promising-looking paths first, so it finds the shortest route without checking every possible path. This is why your RTS units can navigate around buildings and enemies can chase you through mazes.
key_concepts: Nodes: Waypoints the AI can stand on (grid cells or navmesh triangles)
G-cost: Distance from start to current node
H-cost: Estimated distance from current node to goal (heuristic)
F-cost: G + H (total estimated path cost)
Open set: Nodes waiting to be explored
Closed set: Nodes already explored
Heuristic: Guessed distance to goal (usually straight-line)
Admissibility: Heuristic must not overestimate actual distance
Grid vs NavMesh: Grid for 2D, NavMesh for 3D

sections.name: Procedural Content Generation
sections.explanation_simple: Procedural generation is when the computer creates game content automatically instead of a human building it by hand. Think Minecraft - every world is different and generated as you explore. Games like No Man's Sky, Spelunky, and Diablo use procedural generation to create infinite variety. The key insight is that using math (noise functions, random seeds), you can create unique-but-consistent content. The seed number determines everything, so you can share a cool world by sharing just a number.
key_concepts: Seed: A number that determines all random generation (same seed = same result)
Perlin/Simplex Noise: Smooth random-looking patterns (terrain, clouds, textures)
Cellular Automata: Simple rules create complex patterns (caves, water simulation)
Wave Function Collapse: Generates tile patterns from an example (level generation)
L-Systems: Grammar-based plant/tree generation
Voronoi Diagrams: Divides space into regions (biomes, map territories)
BSP Trees: Binary Space Partitioning for dungeon generation
Drunkard's Walk: Random path generation (rivers, corridors)

sections.name: Neural Networks for Game AI
sections.explanation_simple: Neural networks are like the brain of the AI - a web of tiny mathematical 'neurons' that learn from experience. Instead of programming every behavior by hand (like in behavior trees), you show the AI what to do and it figures out how. Think of it like training a dog: you reward good behaviors and punish bad ones, and eventually the AI learns what works. This is called Reinforcement Learning. In games, this is used for things like bot opponents in racing games, enemy AI that adapts to your playstyle, and even entire game characters that learn to move, fight, and make decisions.
key_concepts: Neuron: A single processing unit (takes inputs, applies weights, outputs result)
Layer: A group of neurons (input, hidden, output)
Weights: How important each input is (learned during training)
Activation Function: Makes the output non-linear (ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh)
Forward Pass: Running data through the network to get output
Backpropagation: Adjusting weights based on errors (learning)
Loss Function: How wrong the network's output is
Reinforcement Learning: Agent learns by getting rewards/punishments
Q-Learning: Learning which actions are best in which situations
